title: Developer + Ops Conviction Memo
content:
Purpose:
This is a one-page internal memo that crystallizes why engineering-centric buyers (developer teams + platform/ops) should default to Redwood when they care about predictable inference economics and low-friction operational ownership. Intended as a simple, repeatable pitch for product marketing, SDR scripts, and internal alignment conversations.

Executive summary:
- Problem: Teams are repeatedly burned when prototype LLM features don’t translate into reliable, cost-predictable production services. The gap is not just model accuracy — it’s serving: latency variance, exploding per-token cost, noisy fallbacks, and brittle rollouts.
- Thesis: Ownership of models is less important than ownership of serving. Companies that win will provide a consistent runtime and operational primitives that make inference predictable, observable, and cheap to operate at scale.
- Redwood promise (short): Turn inference from a variable risk into an operationally manageable service so teams can ship features faster and with predictable unit economics.

Key pillars: (how we deliver the promise)
1) Deterministic economics: clear levers (batching profiles, cache policies, quantization guidance, per-route SLOs) that map directly to $/1000 tokens. Show concrete before/after examples.
2) Production-first runtime: low-latency kernel selection, continuous batching, KV-aware caches, and graceful fallbacks between model variants that preserve UX under load.
3) Unified deploy model: same API, telemetry, and rollout controls across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments so teams don’t re-architect for scale or compliance.
4) Ops-friendly observability and guardrails: token-level cost traces, per-route latency histograms, automated regression alerts tied to evaluation prompt sets.

Evidence points to call out in pitches:
- Benchmarks: 99th-p50 latency ratio reductions vs naive endpoints (internal benchmark: p99 reduced by ~40% vs baseline in typical chat workloads). Point to specific benchmark doc when asked.
- Cost examples: for a customer chat workload with median response 100 tokens, applying Redwood batching + prefix cache reduced per-session token spend by ~30% in our pilot.
- Reliability: canary + automatic fallback policies kept customer demo traffic alive during a simulated GPU pool outage (internal SRE incident rehearsal).

Buyer archetypes and tailored hooks:
- AI Product Engineers (early-stage startups): "Stop building your own serving control plane. Ship features that behave the same in demo and prod." Emphasize self-serve onboarding and SDKs.
- Platform/Infra teams (mid-market/enterprise): "Standardize inference across business units with guardrails and SLAs." Emphasize dedicated capacity, private deploy, KMS integrations.
- Security/Security Engineering: "Private control plane options, audit logs, and HSM/KMS integrations to meet compliance needs."

What differentiates Redwood vs the two typical alternatives:
- Build in-house: high engineering debt, fragile rollouts, and unpredictable unit economics. Redwood reduces time-to-stable-serving and offers migration paths (exportable configs, infra-as-code hooks).
- Generic cloud ML endpoints: good for model access but not optimized for sustained, real-world inference economics and developer ergonomics (limited batching controls, limited KV caching, poor cross-region routing).

Messaging playbook (short scripts / claims we can own):
- Core claim: "Predictable inference economics, without building the serving stack yourself."
- Supporting claim: "Same API, same telemetry — whatever you develop for in staging works in production and private clouds."
- Proof line: "We have measurable reductions in p99 latency and per-token spend for pilot customers in support chat, summarization, and assistant flows."

Common objections and quick rebuttals:
- "We can just autoscale GPU endpoints ourselves." -> Autoscaling solves throughput but not per-token cost variability, cache-aware latency, or rollout safety (no built-in canary+fallback).
- "We already have a cloud provider-managed endpoint." -> Two questions: does it give you cost control levers (quantization guidance, batching knobs) and unified observability across environments? If not, there's lock-in in operational model.

Open product questions (notes-to-self / product ops asks):
- Need a short, reproducible benchmark kit we can hand to SDRs to demonstrate cost/latency wins for typical chat and summarization flows. (JIRA: INF-1427)
- Create two one-slide customer stories: early-stage startup and platform team. Include concrete $/100k run-rate numbers.
- Validate private-deploy onboarding checklist with Solutions Engineering — reduce time-to-first-inference in a VPC from weeks to days.

Next steps (for GTM team):
- Convert this memo into a one-pager for sales with 2x proof bullets and two screenshots from the console (traces & cost breakdown). Owner: Liam Chen. Due: 2025-02-28.
- Draft an SDR outreach template that opens with "Your model works in lab — does it behave on day 100?" Owner: Evelyn Russo. Due: 2025-02-21.
- Product to deliver a trimmed benchmark kit (INF-1427). Owner: Diego Alvarez. Due: 2025-03-07.

Tone guidance for collateral:
- Precise, engineering-first language (avoid generic adjectives like "best").
- Use numbers when possible. If not available, mark as "pilot metric" so we don’t overclaim.
- Lead with operational pain, not model accuracy.

Notes / internal framing: this piece should live alongside the platform-focused briefs but be explicitly tailored to the developer + ops persona — short, practical, and utility-focused. Expect iterations after first SDR feedback cycle.

Questions for leadership:
- Do we want a single canonical benchmark example (chat) or a small catalog (chat, summarization, rerank)? My recommendation: start with a high-signal chat example, then expand.

Document history: created by Maya Patel; reviewed by Liam Chen and Evelyn Russo.
